pages.caption: Tropical cyclone · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A tropical cyclone is a rapidly rotating storm system with a low-pressure area, a closed low-level atmospheric circulation, strong winds, and a spiral arrangement of thunderstorms that produce heavy rain and squalls. Depending on its location and strength, a tropical cyclone is called a hurricane, typhoon, tropical storm, cyclonic storm, tropical depression, or simply cyclone.

pages.caption: Tropical cyclone · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A hurricane is a strong tropical cyclone that occurs in the Atlantic Ocean or northeastern Pacific Ocean. A typhoon is the same thing which occurs in the northwestern Pacific Ocean.

pages.caption: Tropical cyclone · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: In the Indian Ocean and South Pacific, comparable storms are referred to as "tropical cyclones". In modern times, on average around 80 to 90 named tropical cyclones form each year around the world, over half of which develop hurricane-force winds of 65 kn or more.

pages.caption: Penguin · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Penguins are a group of flightless semi-aquatic sea birds which live almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere. Only one species, the Galapagos penguin, lives at, and slightly north of, the equator.

pages.caption: Penguin · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Highly adapted for life in the ocean water, penguins have countershaded dark and white plumage and flippers for swimming. Most penguins feed on krill, fish, squid and other forms of sea life which they catch with their bills and swallow whole while swimming.

pages.caption: Penguin · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A penguin has a spiny tongue and powerful jaws to grip slippery prey.

title: METEOR SHOWER
subtitle: Celestial event caused by streams of meteoroids entering Earth's atmosphere

pages.caption: Meteor shower · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A meteor shower is a celestial event in which a number of meteors are observed to radiate, or originate, from one point in the night sky. These meteors are caused by streams of cosmic debris called meteoroids entering Earth's atmosphere at extremely high speeds on parallel trajectories.

pages.caption: Meteor shower · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Most meteors are smaller than a grain of sand, so almost all of them disintegrate and never hit the Earth's surface. Very intense or unusual meteor showers are known as meteor outbursts and meteor storms, which produce at least 1,000 meteors an hour, most notably from the Leonids.

pages.caption: Meteor shower · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: The Meteor Data Centre lists over 900 suspected meteor showers of which about 100 are well established. Several organizations point to viewing opportunities on the Internet.

pages.caption: Meteor shower · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: NASA maintains a daily map of active meteor showers.

pages.caption: Seahorse · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A seahorse is any of 47 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus. Having a head and neck suggestive of a horse, seahorses also feature segmented bony armour, an upright posture and a curled prehensile tail.

pages.caption: Seahorse · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Along with the pipefishes and seadragons they form the family Syngnathidae. They can be found in seas, brackish estuaries and lagoons.

title: COMET
subtitle: Natural object in space that releases gas

pages.caption: Comet · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A comet is an icy, small Solar System body or interstellar object that warms and begins to release gases when passing close to the Sun, a process called outgassing. This produces an extended, gravitationally unbound atmosphere or coma surrounding the nucleus, and sometimes a tail of gas and dust gas blown out from the coma.

pages.caption: Comet · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: These phenomena are due to the effects of solar radiation and the outstreaming solar wind plasma acting upon the nucleus of the comet. Comet nuclei range from a few hundred meters to tens of kilometers across and are composed of loose collections of ice, dust, and small rocky particles.

pages.caption: Comet · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: The coma may be up to 15 times Earth's diameter, while the tail may stretch beyond one astronomical unit. If sufficiently close and bright, a comet may be seen from Earth without the aid of a telescope and can subtend an arc of up to 30° across the sky.

pages.caption: Comet · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Comets have been observed and recorded since ancient times by many cultures and religions.

pages.caption: Mangrove · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A mangrove is a shrub or tree that grows mainly in coastal saline or brackish water. Mangroves grow in an equatorial climate, typically along coastlines and tidal rivers.

pages.caption: Mangrove · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: They have particular adaptations to take in extra oxygen and remove salt, allowing them to tolerate conditions that kill most plants. The term is also used for tropical coastal vegetation consisting of such species.

pages.caption: Mangrove · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Mangroves are taxonomically diverse due to convergent evolution in several plant families. They occur worldwide in tropical and subtropical coastal areas, mainly between latitudes 30° N and 30° S, with the greatest mangrove area within 5° of the equator.

pages.caption: Mangrove · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Mangrove plant families first appeared during the Late Cretaceous to Paleocene epochs and became widely distributed in part due to the movement of tectonic plates. The oldest known fossils of mangrove palm date to 75 million years ago.

pages.caption: Red panda · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: The red panda, also known as the lesser panda, is a small mammal native to the eastern Himalayas and southwestern China. It has dense reddish-brown fur with a black belly and legs, white-lined ears, a mostly white muzzle and a ringed tail.

pages.caption: Red panda · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Its head-to-body length is 51–63. 5 cm (20.

pages.caption: Red panda · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
Red panda · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
Red panda · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: 1 in) tail, and it weighs between 3. 2 and 15 kg.

title: EARTHQUAKE
subtitle: Sudden movement of the Earth's crust

pages.caption: Earthquake · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: An earthquake, also called a quake, tremor, or temblor, is the shaking of the Earth's surface resulting from a sudden release of energy in the lithosphere that creates seismic waves. Earthquakes can range in intensity, from those so weak they cannot be felt, to those violent enough to propel objects and people into the air, damage critical infrastructure, and wreak destruction across entire cities.

pages.caption: Earthquake · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: The seismic activity of an area is the frequency, type, and size of earthquakes experienced over a particular time. The seismicity at a particular location in the Earth is the average rate of seismic energy released per unit volume.

title: MEMORY
subtitle: Faculty of mind to store and retrieve data

pages.caption: Memory · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Memory is the faculty of the mind by which data or information is encoded, stored, and retrieved when needed. It is the retention of information over time for the purpose of influencing future action.

pages.caption: Memory · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: If past events could not be remembered, it would be impossible for language, relationships, or personal identity to develop. Memory loss is usually described as forgetfulness or a disorder such as amnesia.

title: GLACIER
subtitle: Persistent body of ice that moves downhill under its own weight

pages.caption: Glacier · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text:
A glacier is a persistent body of natural ice, a form of
rock, that is constantly moving under its own weight. A glacier forms where the accumulation of snow exceeds its ablation over many years, often centuries.

pages.caption: Glacier · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: It slowly flows and deforms under stresses induced by gravity, undergoing both ductile and brittle deformation, and acquiring distinguishing surface features, such as crevasses and seracs. As a glacier moves, it abrades underlying rock and debris to create glacial landforms, such as cirques, moraines, and fjords.

pages.caption: Glacier · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Although a glacier may flow into a body of water, and can include ice shelves and ice tongues, it originates only on land and is distinct from the much thinner sea ice and lake ice that form on the surface of freezing bodies of water.

pages.caption: Mars · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. It is also known as the "Red Planet", for its orange-red appearance.

pages.caption: Mars · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Mars is a desert-like rocky planet with a tenuous atmosphere that is primarily carbon dioxide. At the average surface level the atmospheric pressure is a few thousandths of Earth's, atmospheric temperature ranges from −153 to 20 °C, and cosmic radiation is high.

pages.caption: Mars · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Mars retains some water, in the ground as well as thinly in the atmosphere, forming cirrus clouds, fog, frost, larger polar regions of permafrost and ice caps, but no bodies of liquid surface water. Its surface gravity is roughly a third of Earth's or double that of the Moon.

pages.caption: Mars · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Its mean diameter, 6,779 km (4,212 mi), is about half the Earth's, or twice the Moon's, and its surface area is around the size of all the dry land of Earth.

title: PHOTOSYNTHESIS
subtitle: Biological process to convert light into chemical energy

pages.caption: Photosynthesis · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Photosynthesis is a system of biological processes by which photopigment-bearing autotrophic organisms, such as most plants, algae and cyanobacteria, convert light energy—typically from sunlight—into the chemical energy necessary to fuel their metabolism. The term photosynthesis usually refers to oxygenic photosynthesis, a process that releases oxygen as a byproduct of water splitting.

pages.caption: Photosynthesis · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Photosynthetic organisms store the converted chemical energy within the bonds of intracellular organic compounds, typically carbohydrates like sugars, starches, phytoglycogen and cellulose. When needing to use this stored energy, an organism's cells then metabolize the organic compounds through cellular respiration.

pages.caption: Photosynthesis · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Photosynthesis plays a critical role in producing and maintaining the oxygen content of the Earth's atmosphere, and it supplies most of the biological energy necessary for complex life on Earth.

title: DOLPHIN
subtitle: Informal classification of marine mammals, closely related to whales and porpoises

pages.caption: Dolphin · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A dolphin is any one of the 40 extant species of aquatic mammal from the cetacean families Delphinidae, Platanistidae, Iniidae, Pontoporiidae, and the probably extinct Lipotidae. All these families belong to the parvorder Odontoceti, i.

pages.caption: Dolphin · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: e. , toothed whales, which also include the closely related families Monodontidae and Phocoenidae (porpoises), as well as the more distant families Physeteroidea and Ziphiidae.

pages.caption: Antarctica · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Antarctica is Earth's southernmost and least-populated continent. Situated almost entirely south of the Antarctic Circle and surrounded by the Southern Ocean, it contains the geographic South Pole.

pages.caption: Antarctica · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Antarctica is the fifth-largest continent, being about 40% larger than Europe, and has an area of 14,200,000 km2 (5,500,000 sq mi). Most of Antarctica is covered by the Antarctic ice sheet, with an average thickness of 1.

pages.caption: Antarctica · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
Saturn · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun, and is the second largest planet in the Solar System, after Jupiter. It is a gas giant, with an average radius of about 9 times that of Earth.

pages.caption: Saturn · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: It has an eighth of the average density of Earth, but is over 95 times more massive. Even though Saturn is almost as big as Jupiter, it has less than a third of its mass.

pages.caption: Saturn · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Saturn orbits the Sun at a distance of 9. 59 AU (1,434 million km), with an orbital period of 29.

pages.caption: Saturn · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: 45 years.

title: SOLAR ECLIPSE
subtitle: Event wherein the Sun is obscured by the Moon

pages.caption: Solar eclipse · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, thereby obscuring the view of the Sun from a small part of Earth, totally or partially. Such an alignment occurs approximately every six months, during the eclipse season in its new moon phase, when the Moon's orbital plane is closest to the plane of Earth's orbit.

pages.caption: Solar eclipse · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: In a total eclipse, the disk of the Sun is fully obscured by the Moon. In partial and annular eclipses, only part of the Sun is obscured.

pages.caption: Solar eclipse · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Unlike a lunar eclipse, which may be viewed from anywhere on the night side of Earth, a solar eclipse can only be viewed from a relatively small area of the world. As such, although total solar eclipses occur somewhere on Earth every 18 months on average, they recur at any given place only once every 360 to 410 years.

title: VOLCANO
subtitle: Rupture in a planet's crust where material escapes

pages.caption: Volcano · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A volcano is a vent or fissure in the crust of a planetary-mass object that allows hot lava, volcanic ash, and gases to escape from a magma chamber below the surface. On Earth, volcanoes are most often found where tectonic plates are diverging or converging, and because most of Earth's plate boundaries are underwater, most volcanoes are found underwater.

pages.caption: Volcano · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: For example, a mid-ocean ridge, such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, has volcanoes caused by divergent tectonic plates whereas the Pacific Ring of Fire has volcanoes caused by convergent tectonic plates. Volcanoes resulting from divergent tectonic activity are usually non-explosive whereas those resulting from convergent tectonic activity cause violent eruptions.

pages.caption: Volcano · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: Volcanoes can also form where there is stretching and thinning of the crust's plates, such as in the East African Rift, the Wells Gray-Clearwater volcanic field, and the Rio Grande rift in North America. Volcanism away from plate boundaries most likely arises from upwelling diapirs from the core–mantle boundary called mantle plumes, 3,000 kilometres (1,900 mi) deep within Earth.

pages.caption: Volcano · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: This results in hotspot volcanism or intraplate volcanism, in which the plume may cause thinning of the crust and result in a volcanic island chain due to the continuous movement of the tectonic plate, of which the Hawaiian hotspot is an example. Volcanoes are usually not created at transform tectonic boundaries where two tectonic plates slide past one another.

pages.caption: Black hole · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: A black hole is an astronomical body so compact that its gravity prevents anything, including light, from escaping. Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, which describes gravitation as the curvature of spacetime, predicts that any sufficiently compact mass will form a black hole.

pages.caption: Black hole · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: The boundary of no escape is called the event horizon. In general relativity, crossing a black hole's event horizon traps an object inside but produces no locally detectable change.

pages.caption: Black hole · Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia; image license and author: see source
pages.text: General relativity also predicts that every black hole should have a central singularity, where the curvature of spacetime is infinite.

title: WHY DOES THE MOON ALWAYS SHOW US THE SAME FACE?
subtitle: A curious story about the rhythm of our closest neighbour

pages.caption: Earth and the Moon are linked by gravity.
pages.text: Have you ever noticed that the Moon seems to show us the same face every night? It is not a coincidence. The Moon rotates on its axis at almost exactly the same rate as it travels around Earth.

pages.caption: Gravity shapes the motion of objects in space.
pages.text: This remarkable pattern is called tidal locking. Over billions of years, Earth’s gravity gradually slowed the Moon’s rotation until the two movements became synchronized.

pages.caption: Sunlight reaches different parts of the Moon.
pages.text: That does not mean the far side of the Moon is always dark. It receives sunlight just like the side we see. The phrase “dark side” is therefore a little misleading.

pages.caption: Space exploration continues to reveal new discoveries.
pages.text: The Moon still has many secrets. Space missions have helped scientists understand its surface, but new discoveries continue to change what we know about our nearest celestial neighbour.

title: WHY DO WE DREAM?
subtitle: A journey into the stories our minds create at night

pages.caption: Sleep is an active time for the brain.
pages.text: Every night, our minds create strange stories while we sleep. Some dreams feel surprisingly real, while others disappear as soon as we wake up. Scientists are still exploring why we dream.

pages.caption: Memories and emotions may influence our dreams.
pages.text: One idea is that dreams help us process memories and emotions. During sleep, the brain organizes information from the day and may connect experiences in unexpected ways.

pages.caption: A new morning often makes a dream harder to remember.
pages.text: We do not remember every dream. Our ability to recall a dream depends partly on when we wake up and how quickly we pay attention to it. Keeping a notebook nearby may help.

title: HOW DO TREES COMMUNICATE?
subtitle: The surprising connections beneath a forest floor

pages.caption: A forest is full of hidden connections.
pages.text: A forest may look quiet, but trees are constantly responding to their surroundings. Through their roots and relationships with fungi, plants can exchange resources and chemical signals.

pages.caption: Fungi can form networks around plant roots.
pages.text: Tiny fungal threads can connect with tree roots. These partnerships help plants absorb nutrients from the soil. Researchers study how resources sometimes move through these underground networks.

pages.caption: There is still much to learn about forest ecosystems.
pages.text: It is tempting to imagine trees talking like people, but the science is more complex. Understanding these connections helps us appreciate how many living things depend on one another.

title: AURORA
subtitle: Atmospheric effect caused by the solar wind

pages.caption: Aurora · Image from Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (see source for attribution)
pages.text: An aurora is a natural light display in Earth's upper atmosphere caused by charged particles from the Sun colliding with atoms in the atmosphere. These collisions excite oxygen and nitrogen, which then emit light of different colours such as green, red, and purple.

pages.caption: Aurora · Image from Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (see source for attribution)
pages.text: When observed in high-latitude regions they are called polar lights and aurora polaris. In the Arctic they are called the northern lights or aurora borealis; in the Antarctic, the term southern lights or aurora australis is used.

pages.caption: Aurora · Image from Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (see source for attribution)
pages.text: Auroras display dynamic patterns of radiant light that appear as curtains, rays, spirals or dynamic flickers covering the entire sky.

pages.caption: Octopus · Image from Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (see source for attribution)
pages.text: An octopus is a soft-bodied, eight-limbed mollusc of the order Octopoda. The order consists of some 300 species and is grouped within the class Cephalopoda with squids, cuttlefish, and nautiloids.

pages.caption: Octopus · Image from Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (see source for attribution)
pages.text: Like other cephalopods, an octopus is bilaterally symmetric with two eyes and a beaked mouth at the centre point of the eight limbs. An octopus can radically deform its shape, enabling it to squeeze through small gaps.

pages.caption: Octopus · Image from Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (see source for attribution)
pages.text: They trail their appendages behind them as they swim backwards. The siphon is used for respiration and locomotion.

pages.caption: Octopus · Image from Wikimedia Commons / Wikipedia (see source for attribution)
pages.text: Octopuses have a complex nervous system and excellent sight, and are among the most intelligent and behaviourally diverse invertebrates.

title: BIOLUMINESCENCE
subtitle: Emission of light by a living organism

pages.caption: Bioluminescence · Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (see source for attribution)
pages.text: Bioluminescence is the production of light by an organism as the result of a chemiluminescence reaction. It occurs in a wide variety of organisms, including marine vertebrates and invertebrates, terrestrial arthropods such as fireflies, some fungi, and microorganisms such as some bacteria and dinoflagellates.

pages.caption: Bioluminescence · Wikipedia / Wikimedia Commons (see source for attribution)
pages.text: In some animals, the light is bacteriogenic, produced by symbiotic bacteria such as those from the genus Vibrio; in others, it is autogenic, produced by the animals themselves. Bioluminescence has evolved independently at least 94 times, first emerging in octocorals some 540 million years ago.
